steps.why: This proof starts by SPLITTING the pair into its two separate lines with unknown coefficients, then matching coefficients against the given equation. Those matched coefficients, linking (a, h, b) to the two lines, are what every later step uses.

Dividing by a instead of b.
steps.memory_tip: The pair passes through the ORIGIN, so O is one vertex for free. Split the pair in slope form.

steps.why: A homogeneous second-degree equation represents a pair of lines through the ORIGIN (real lines when h² ≥ ab), so the third vertex is free — which is what shortens the area formula to ½|x₁y₂ − x₂y₁|.
common_mistakes: Drawing the pair away from the origin, which a homogeneous equation cannot represent.
Drawing the cutting line through the origin too, which would give no triangle.
steps.memory_tip: The picture makes it visible that only TWO vertices have to be found.

steps.margin_note: One mark. One vertex is where the given line meets the first of the two lines — solve that pair by cross-multiplication, keeping everything in letters.

steps.margin_note: The last mark. m₂ − m₁ cannot be written from (1) directly, but (m₂ − m₁)² = (m₁+m₂)² − 4m₁m₂ can — so square the difference first, then substitute (1) and clear the b's.

steps.why: Only the SUM and PRODUCT of the slopes are known, never the slopes themselves — so any expression in them must first be written through those two, which is what the identity does.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that b appears in both numerator and denominator and cancels.
steps.memory_tip: m₂ − m₁ cannot be written from (1) directly, but (m₁+m₂)² − 4m₁m₂ can — so SQUARE the difference first.
lines_compact: [∵ |p − q| = √((p + q)² − 4pq), applied to p = m₁, q = m₂]

insider_note: Only the SUM and PRODUCT of the slopes are needed, never the slopes themselves: m₁ + m₂ = −2h/b, m₁m₂ = a/b. Write m₂ − m₁ as √((m₁+m₂)² − 4m₁m₂), and the b cancels top and bottom at the end.
